newsitem.title: USA: IBM CFO optimistic about rest of year.
newsitem.headline: IBM CFO optimistic about rest of year.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp Chief Financial Officer G. Richard Thoman on Wednesday said he "feels good" about the rest of the year, as more revenues come from the company's fastest-growing businesses.
"We feel good about the whole year," Thoman told analysts in a meeting/conference call after IBM reported first-quarter earnings of $2.37 a share, surpassing most Wall Street estimates.
"We believe (the quarter) demonstrates the breadth in the IBM business portfolio," Thoman said.

Thoman told analysts that the stronger dollar had a negative impact of $0.19 a share on its earnings. He said that if the dollar stayed at current exchange rates against foreign currencies, IBM would continue to feel a negative impact.
He said that impact may ease in the latter part of the year, but that depended on the dollar's strength.
"The currency issues we dealt with in the first quarter will be here all year," Thoman said.
He said IBM expected a tax rate of less than 34 percent for the full year, down from 35.5 percent in the first quarter, but he could not provide an exact rate yet.

Thoman said a positive impact from a lower tax rate and fewer shares outstanding should offset the expected negative impact of currency translations. As a result, he advised analysts not to change their 1997 earnings estimates.
"I'm comfortable that you should not change your models for '97," Thoman said. "I'm comfortable with where you are."
In IBM's hardware businesses, he said mainframes and AS/400 minicomputers were a disappointment.

Mainframe revenues declined, but Thoman did not say by how much. The AS/400 minicomputer business is expected to recover a bit in the second quarter and even more in the second half of the year, with some product introductions, Thoman said.
In the personal computer business, Thoman said IBM outperformed Compaq Computer Corp in unit shipments and revenue growth, although it still lagged the world's leading PC maker in profit margins.
A decline in memory chip prices was a big reason for lower gross profit margins on hardware, though Thoman said most of the negative impact from memory prices was "behind us."

Thoman emphasized that IBM was generating more growth from businesses outside the hardware area. He said its higher-end server businesses -- mainframes, minicomputers and workstations -- contributed only 11 percent of total revenues in the first quarter versus 17 percent in 1994. Meanwhile, the company's services business contributed about 24 percent of total first-quarter revenues versus about 15 percent in 1994.

Revenues from services rose 28 percent in the first quarter, but Thoman cautioned that the business could not sustain that rate. Still, he said growth in that segment would outpace the industry as a whole.
